strengths: Practical and efficient adaptation approach: MusicInfuser conditions a pre-trained T2V diffusion model (Mochi) on music using lightweight components (zero-initialized cross-attention, higher-rank LoRA) trained on a single A100 for ~20 hours, which is attractive for reproducibility and code release.

Well-motivated design choices addressing the modality-gap problem: zero-initialized output projection to preserve base-model knowledge, higher LoRA rank justified by spatiotemporal complexity, Beta-to-Uniform noise scheduling, layer-adaptability-based placement of cross-attention, and in-the-wild data mixing with caption diversification.

Good qualitative demonstrations of generality: group choreography via prompt editing (Fig. 2), tempo-controlled dance via time-stretched music (Fig. 6), generalization to unseen SUNO AI music and 2x longer videos (Figs. 3, 7), and seed-diversity results (Fig. 8), supported by a comprehensive supplementary with prompts, evaluation system prompts, layer-adaptability analysis, and failure cases.

Honest reporting: the paper acknowledges that ground-truth AIST data outperforms their model on several metrics, discusses limitations (fine details, silhouette issues), and situates the work relative to concurrent efforts (VideoJAM, OmniHuman-1).
Systematic ablation study (Table 4) covering each proposed component, including a reasonable feature-addition baseline for the ZICA adapter.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-judge scores (VideoLLaMA 2) with no human study and no validation that these scores correlate with human judgment. Reported differences between methods are small (often 0.1–0.3 on a 10-point scale) with no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance reported, making many of the quantitative claims weakly supported. Established, objective dance/video metrics (e.g., beat F1 from the AIST++ literature, FVD/FGD) are notably absent, especially given that beat alignment is a central claimed contribution.

Baseline comparisons are arguably unfair: MM-Diffusion (2023) is a much older, lower-capacity model trained on different data, and Mochi cannot hear music, so the dance-quality comparison mostly demonstrates the trivial gap between music-conditioned and unconditioned generation. No comparison with recent strong audio-driven human video generation systems is provided.

The HR-LoRA rationale is hand-wavy: the homography 8-DOF argument does not rigorously establish an optimal rank for video adaptation, and no rank sweep is reported (only rank 64 is used). The Beta-Uniform scheduling motivation conflates noise levels with frequency content loosely, and its ablation actually worsens style/beat alignment while improving body representation, suggesting a trade-off that is not analyzed.

The in-the-wild YouTube training data (15,799 clips) is described only briefly, without details on quality filtering, licensing considerations, or its effect measured in isolation beyond a single Table 3 row.

Some claims (e.g., 'superior alignment between music beat patterns and dance movements, visible in the correspondence between spectrogram intensity and motion transitions') rest on qualitative visual inspection of static figure strips, which the authors themselves note under-samples motion relative to the beat frequency; no quantitative synchronization evidence is provided in the paper itself.

Layer-adaptability selection (top 16 of 48 layers via STG/VBench) is presented as the largest ablation contributor but the underlying selection procedure and its sensitivity are deferred to supplementary with limited analysis.

strengths: The core idea of adapting a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model to music conditioning with lightweight adapters (zero-initialized cross-attention plus LoRA) is sensible and practical, and avoids the significant cost of training joint audio-video models from scratch.

The paper avoids dependence on motion capture data, training only on dance videos (AIST plus in-the-wild YouTube data), which improves scalability and apparent generalization to unseen music genres (SUNO AI 'K-pop' tracks) and longer-than-trained sequences.

An ablation study (Table 4) is provided that isolates each proposed component (ZICA layer selection, higher-rank LoRA, Beta-Uniform scheduling, feature-addition baseline), and the code and project page are stated to be released, aiding reproducibility.

Useful qualitative behaviors are demonstrated: tempo-responsive motion (Fig. 6), group choreography via prompt (Fig. 2), seed diversity (Fig. 8), and an honest limitations section covering failure cases.
The paper is generally well written and clearly organized, with architecture, training recipe (single A100, 4,000 steps), and prompts/evaluation system prompts disclosed in the supplementary.
weaknesses: The entire quantitative evaluation rests on unvalidated LLM-based scoring (VideoLLaMA 2 asked to output 0-10 ratings). No human study, no inter-annotator agreement, and no correlation analysis between the Video-LLM scores and human judgment are provided. LLM-as-judge for fine-grained temporal properties like beat alignment of dance is exactly the kind of judgment current Video-LLMs are least reliable at, and no standard objective dance metrics (e.g., beat hit rate, FID-k, diversity scores used in the music-to-dance literature) are reported.

The quantitative margins over baselines are very small relative to the noise floor of such an evaluation: e.g., dance quality average 7.95 vs. 7.70 for the base Mochi model (Table 1), with no variance, confidence intervals, or number of trials reported. Only 100 videos (10 prompts x 10 tracks) are evaluated per configuration, so differences of ~0.1-0.3 on a 10-point scale are unlikely to be statistically meaningful.

The baseline comparison is thin. The only real conditioned baseline is MM-Diffusion (a 2023 model for joint audio-video generation, not designed for dance), plus the unmodified base model Mochi. No comparison is attempted with the substantial music-to-dance generation literature (e.g., EDGE, Bailando, FACT) even via proxy metrics, so the claimed improvement over 'prior work' is largely asserted rather than measured.

Novelty of the individual technical components is limited: zero-initialized output projection in a new cross-attention layer is a well-established technique (e.g., IP-Adapter-style conditioning), and 'HR-LoRA' amounts to using rank 64 instead of 8-16. The theoretical justification (Sec. 4.2) is hand-wavy - the homography rank-8 argument is heuristic and unsupported by analysis or experiments. Beta-Uniform scheduling contributes marginally and its mechanism is not rigorously analyzed.

There is a mismatch between the paper's claims and the evidence for synchronization: beat alignment is a central claim, yet the main figures concede that motion appears slower due to frame sampling, and beat synchronization can only truly be verified from the project page videos. The in-paper visual evidence (flattened frame strips) cannot support claims about rhythmic alignment.

Table 1 reveals the method scores below ground truth on body representation (7.16 vs 7.53) and below the plain Mochi baseline on body representation (7.47), while the text claims 'maintaining competitive scores' - the presentation glosses over unfavorable results.

Some methodology details that materially affect results are deferred or under-specified: the layer-selection criterion is borrowed from STG with only a brief note, the exact Beta scheduling decay is stated only as 'exponential decay toward 1', and the in-the-wild data collection (YouTube scraping) raises questions about data curation, licensing, and quality filtering that are not addressed.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated contribution: adapting a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model (Mochi) to music conditioning via lightweight adapters (ZICA cross-attention + HR-LoRA) avoids training a costly joint audio-video model and requires only dance videos, not motion capture — a meaningful simplification over prior music-to-dance work (EDGE, Bailando, FACT, etc.).

Several sensible design components with individual rationale: zero-initialized output projection to preserve the base prior, layer-adaptability-based selection of cross-attention placement (informed by STG), Beta-to-Uniform noise scheduling for curriculum-style fine-tuning, caption diversification to reduce text reliance, and mixing in-the-wild YouTube data for regularization.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4) isolating each component, plus qualitative ablations in the supplementary; the feature-addition baseline confirms the value of cross-attention over naive conditioning.

Good breadth of empirical demonstrations: text+music controllability (Fig. 1), group choreography via prompt modification (Fig. 2), 2x longer videos and unseen music genres (Figs. 3, 7), tempo sensitivity (Fig. 6), and seed diversity (Fig. 8), which together support the generalization claims.

Introduces a reusable Video-LLM-based evaluation protocol (Table 8) that jointly assesses dance quality, video quality, and prompt alignment; the transparency of publishing the exact rating prompts aids reproducibility.
Code and project page released; clear writing with honest limitations section (finger/face failures, silhouette artifacts) and a discussion of concurrent work (VideoJAM, OmniHuman-1).
weaknesses: The entire quantitative evaluation rests on VideoLLaMA 2 ratings of only 100 generated videos (10 prompts x 10 tracks) per configuration, with no human study, no variance across seeds, and no standard metrics (e.g., FVD, beat-hit/F1-k on detected beats, FGD on pose estimates). LLM-judge scores on narrow 0.1-0.3 point differences (Tables 1-4) are not obviously meaningful, and there is a circularity risk in using a generative VLM to grade generative outputs. The ablation gains in particular (~0.1-0.2 on a 10-point scale) may be within evaluation noise.

Beat alignment — the core claim — is never verified objectively (no beat-detection analysis or temporal alignment of motion onsets to audio beats); the claim rests on LLM judgments and qualitative spectrogram-vs-frame correspondences in static figures.

The motivation for HR-LoRA is loosely argued: the claim that video adaptation requires higher rank via a homography degree-of-freedom argument is hand-wavy, and the ablation actually shows rank-64 LoRA slightly hurts video quality (8.99 vs 8.96 overall) while helping dance quality — a mixed result the text glosses over. Similarly, Beta-Uniform scheduling lowers style alignment (8.04 -> 7.56) and beat alignment (9.07 -> 8.89) while improving only body representation, yet is presented as a clear win.

Baseline comparison is thin: the only conditional baseline is MM-Diffusion, a 2023 low-resolution joint audio-video model that is not a strong contemporary reference, and Mochi-without-music is not a fair competitor on music-conditioned metrics. No comparison against state-of-the-art commercial systems or recent concurrent audio-conditioned video generation, and no discussion of why motion-skeleton-then-rendering pipelines were not compared end-to-end.

The AIST GT row is described as an 'upper bound' for some metrics, yet the method beats GT on style alignment (7.56 vs 7.46) and choreography complexity (7.90 vs 7.45), which undercuts confidence in the metric's calibration rather than supporting the paper's claims.

Training/evaluation is confined to AIST's studio, single-dancer, front-view distribution plus loosely curated YouTube clips; robustness to crowded scenes, occlusion, or non-dance music is untested, and the 2.5-second training clips are short relative to the claimed long-video generalization.

strengths: Practical and resource-efficient contribution: adapting a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model (Mochi) with LoRA and injected ZICA blocks achieves music-conditioned dance generation with training on a single A100 in ~20 hours, avoiding motion capture data entirely — a compelling alternative to training multimodal audio-video models from scratch.

The layer adaptability criterion (Sec. 4.1) is a genuinely interesting idea: measuring each layer's positive influence via layer-skip guidance rather than removal-based importance is principled, and Table 1/Table 5 show it outperforms uniform, first/middle/last-layer, and even all-layer selection strategies.

Comprehensive ablation studies covering layer selection, Beta-Uniform scheduling, zero-init cross-attention, LoRA rank, and feature addition, with results cross-validated using two different Video-LLM judges (Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2) showing consistent trends (Tables 1, 5, 6).

Thorough validation of the proposed evaluation protocol: ground-truth AIST videos act as an upper bound on dance-quality metrics, and human A/B evaluation (33 participants) qualitatively supports the automatic metric rankings.

Demonstrated generalization beyond the training distribution: unseen subjects (animals), longer videos (up to 9s vs ~2.5s training clips), SUNO-generated K-pop music, tempo-modulation responsiveness (Fig. 7), and seed-based diversity (Fig. 8). Honest limitations section acknowledging inherited artifacts.

Well-documented reproducibility details: training hyperparameters, dataset construction, test music tracks, prompt templates, and full evaluation system prompts are all provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evidence rests on a self-proposed Video-LLM judging metric that the authors themselves design and tune. LLM judges are known to exhibit biases (e.g., favoring the outputs of similar-generation systems, sensitivity to prompt phrasing). While the GT upper-bound check and human evaluation partially mitigate this, no established, standard music-dance alignment metrics (e.g., beat-hit F1/FKD used in the music-to-dance literature) are reported, making cross-paper comparison impossible.

Baseline comparison is thin: the only trained baseline is MM-Diffusion (CVPR 2023), which is far behind the state of the art. Comparisons with skeleton-based methods (EDGE) are only qualitative (Fig. 2), and there is no comparison against stronger recent motion-then-render pipelines or concurrent music-conditioned video approaches, so the claim of 'outperforming baseline models' is weakly supported.

Several reported gains are small and potentially within noise: e.g., in Table 2 MusicInfuser's dance quality average (7.95) is close to ground truth (8.01) and to Mochi (7.70); Table 4 style capture (7.80) is actually lower than the Mochi baseline (7.98). No variance/standard deviations or significance tests are reported anywhere.

The layer adaptability score is ultimately derived from VBench imaging quality via an inference-time guidance method (STG); the connection between 'imaging quality when a layer is used as guidance' and 'suitability for music conditioning' is intuitive but heuristic, and no analysis is given of how robust the selected layers are to the choice of metric or model.

Novelty is incremental in parts: zero-initialized cross-attention and LoRA are established techniques, and the layer-skip guidance formulation is adapted from prior work (SAG, skip guidance, STG). The Beta-Uniform schedule is simple and its ablation gains (Table 6) are mixed depending on the judge model.

The claim that text-to-video models 'already know how to dance' and the framing against motion-data-free training are somewhat overstated: the training set itself consists of dance videos (AIST + YouTube dance playlists), so the model does learn music-dance association from dance-specific data.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('cateory' in Fig. 6 caption, 'in the middle of a New York City'), and Fig. 9's human evaluation reports raw preference percentages without any statistical detail (number of comparisons per question, confidence intervals).

strengths: Practical and efficient contribution: adapting a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model (Mochi) to music conditioning with zero-initialized cross-attention and LoRA, trained on a single A100 in ~20 hours, is a useful demonstration that motion capture data and skeleton representations can be bypassed for dance video generation.

The layer adaptability criterion (Sec. 4.1) is a reasonably novel, computationally feasible approach to choosing which DiT blocks to equip with cross-attention, and it is supported by ablations (Tables 1 and 5) showing it outperforms even 'All Layers' adaptation.

Beta-Uniform noise scheduling is a simple, plausible idea for preserving pretrained denoising capability during adapter training, and its ablation shows a measurable (if modest) effect on body representation and movement realism.

The proposed Video-LLM-based evaluation protocol is transparently documented (exact prompts in Table 10), tested with two different judges (Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2 showing similar trends), and sanity-checked against ground truth (Tables 2-3), with a 33-participant human A/B study (Fig. 9) showing clear margins over MM-Diffusion.

Good breadth of qualitative demonstrations: text+music compositionality (Fig. 1), unseen subjects (Fig. 3), tempo responsiveness (Fig. 7), longer-than-training videos with unseen music (Fig. 6), and honest failure cases (Fig. 17).
weaknesses: Weak baseline set and missing quantitative comparison with the most relevant prior work. Quantitative tables (2-3) compare only against MM-Diffusion (2023, low-resolution joint audio-video model) and unconditioned Mochi. EDGE [44] is discussed in Fig. 2 and referenced in the supplementary, but no quantitative music-to-dance metrics (e.g., beat F-score as in AIST++/EDGE) are reported against any skeleton-based or recent music-conditioned method, weakening the 'outperforming baselines' claim.

The evaluation is largely self-referential. The primary metrics are Video-LLM scores with self-designed prompts; the measured margins over Mochi are small (dance quality 7.95 vs 7.70; prompt alignment 8.96 vs 8.86) with no variance or significance testing over the 100 generated videos. Notably, ground truth scores (Table 2) are barely above or sometimes below the model's own scores (style alignment 7.46 GT vs 7.56 Ours; beat alignment 8.95 vs 8.89), which either undermines the metric's discriminative validity or suggests scores are compressed near the top of the scale.

Human evaluation is only conducted against MM-Diffusion, the weakest baseline; no human study against Mochi fine-tuned variants or layer-selection ablations is provided, so the most interesting design choices are validated only by LLM judges.

The layer adaptability criterion has a tenuous connection to its target use: adaptability is computed from imaging/aesthetic quality of base-model generations under skip guidance (Fig. 15, supplementary), yet it is used to select layers for audio conditioning. Why imaging quality of audio-free generations predicts which layers best absorb music conditioning is asserted intuitively rather than analyzed (e.g., no analysis of what the selected layers do, or correlation between adaptability ranking and fine-tuned performance).

Ablation gains are small and evaluated with the same LLM-based metric whose reliability is itself part of the contribution, creating a circularity risk; differences of ~0.1-0.3 on a 10-point scale (Tables 5-6) are hard to interpret without error bars or judge-robustness analysis.

Reproducibility concerns: the in-the-wild training data is described only as '4 YouTube playlists' with no identifiable source, captions are generated by VideoChat2, and no code/model release is mentioned in the manuscript.

Presentation issues: Table 1 and Table 2 report different overall scores for 'Ours' (8.14 vs 7.95) under what appear to be different prompt sets without clear in-text explanation; typos ('cateory', 'roo.op'); the motivating claim that skeletal representations are 'underparameterized' (Fig. 2) is qualitative and never quantitatively tested against a video-based metric.

The methodological novelty is largely compositional (zero-init cross-attention, LoRA, feature-addition baselines are all established); the genuinely new elements (adaptability selection, Beta-Uniform scheduling) provide modest, narrowly measured gains, making the paper closer to a well-executed system demonstration than a substantial methodological advance.

strengths: Practically valuable direction: adapting a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model (Mochi) to music conditioning, rather than training audio-video generative models from scratch, is efficient (single GPU, ~20 hours, 4k steps) and avoids motion capture, addressing a real gap between music-to-dance skeleton methods and video-level generation.

The layer adaptability criterion (Sec. 4.1) is a principled and interesting idea: using a layer as guidance while the remaining model provides the base denoiser avoids out-of-distribution fine-tuning of every layer combination, and the ablations (Tables 1, 5) support that the selected layers outperform even full-layer adaptation.

The proposed Video-LLM-based evaluation protocol is validated in a meaningful way: ground-truth AIST data scores as an upper bound on beat alignment and movement realism (Tables 2-3), and human A/B evaluation with 33 participants (Fig. 9) shows correlation with the automatic metrics.

Comprehensive ablations across ZICA initialization, LoRA rank, Beta-Uniform scheduling, in-the-wild data, and prompt diversification, with trends replicated under two different judge models (Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2, Table 5-6), increasing confidence that gains are not an artifact of a single evaluator.

Demonstrated generalization beyond the training distribution: unseen music genres (SUNO-generated), longer videos, unseen subjects (animals, Figs. 3, 6), tempo manipulation (Fig. 7), and seed diversity (Fig. 8) provide evidence the model learns music-motion coupling rather than memorizing choreographies.
Limitations are candidly discussed (supplementary Sec. D), including inherited failure modes from the base model.
weaknesses: The layer adaptability criterion is computed with VBench imaging/aesthetic quality of the base model (supplementary Sec. G), i.e., a metric of generic video structure, not of music-motion alignment. The rationale connecting 'high imaging quality when used as guidance' to 'suitable for cross-attention music injection' is heuristic; the paper would benefit from analysis of what the selected layers actually do, and the criterion's generality beyond this specific model/dataset is unclear.

Quantitative margins are small and reported without variance or statistical significance. For example, in Table 2 MusicInfuser scores 7.95 vs. 7.90 (Mochi) and 7.76 (MM-Diffusion) on dance quality average, and several ablation deltas in Tables 1 and 4 are within 0.2-0.3 points; given 100 evaluation videos per configuration, these gaps may not be reliable.

Baseline comparisons are limited and somewhat dated: MM-Diffusion (CVPR 2023) is a joint audio-video model not designed for this task, and the strongest skeleton-based work (EDGE) is relegated to qualitative comparison. No comparison against concurrent audio-conditioned video generation approaches is quantitative.

The evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-judge and human A/B preference; no standard objective metrics (FVD, beat-F1/kbd consistency used in music-dance literature, e.g., AIST++ benchmarks) are reported, making it hard to compare with prior music-to-dance work on equal footing.

The Beta-Uniform scheduling is motivated narratively (fine-to-coarse adaptation) but lacks direct evidence; the ablation effect is mixed across judge models (it improves body representation but slightly lowers style/beat alignment in Table 6), and the choice of initial beta=3 is unexplained.
Only one base model (Mochi) is evaluated, so it remains open whether the layer-selection and adaptation recipe transfer to other video diffusion architectures.

The in-the-wild training data (YouTube playlists, ~15.8k clips) raises dataset licensing/provenance questions that are not discussed, and details of its curation are deferred to supplementary material.

Minor presentation issues: small metric deltas not contextualized, some typos ('cateory', 'roo.op'), and the claim that layer adaptability 'eliminates the need to train separate video models' could be stated more carefully since the criterion still requires sampling with 48 layer-skipped variants.
